forefront: If there is no compulsion in religion, why do apostasy statutes still stand — and who benefits from keeping them on the books?
healthy: No intermediary stands between the believer and God, and for centuries scholars refused state payroll to preserve their independence.
history: There is no central 'church', and authority is distributed among scholars, states and communities.
law: What Muslims everywhere share is a set of legal questions each state answers differently.
money: State-administered zakat and waqf boards concentrate assets under government-appointed managers with recurring corruption findings.
reach: Corporal punishment in some madrasa contexts, and abuse within residential religious schools, is documented and under-prosecuted.
techniques: Thirty named techniques from domestic-abuse and social-psychology research, applied to institutions, in the eight stages of the cycle.
loops: The seven loops below show how the practices connect, so that each step makes the next one easier and the last step feeds the first.
say-do: Abuse cases in religious schools were handled as community matters, with the teacher relocated rather than reported.
cost: Marriage, custody, and inheritance law in many jurisdictions is conditioned on religious status.
ledger: Government religious ministries benefit, employing hundreds of thousands and controlling sermon content.
who-gets-hurt: The table names who carries the most, how, and what makes it worse.
